textbookText: Activity: 8.12 Objective: To identify the heart and its external feature. Apparatus required: dissecting tray, forceps, needle, blade, magnifying glass Procedure: i. Lay down a chloroformed or freshly preserved frog in dissecting dish ventro-dorsally i.e. ventral surface facing up. ii. Fix the frog by pinning through the limbs. iii. Dissect open the body cavity and identify heart. iv. Observe with the help of magnifying glass. v. Draw and note down the external features for discussion. Conclusion: A. HEART 1. External features The heart of a frog is a dark red colored and conical muscular organ with a broad anterior side and somewhat tapered posterior side. It is protected dorsally by vertebral column and ventrolaterally by the pectoral girdle. It lies mid-ventrally in the anterior body cavity in between two lungs, just anterior to the liver. It is enclosed within a delicate, thin and transparent two layered sac called the pericardium. The outer layer is parietal pericardium and inner layer is known as visceral pericardium. A space or cavity between these two layers is called the pericardial cavity which is filled with a pericardial fluid. The pericardial fluid maintains the heart moist, reduces friction and allows its free movements; also protect from the shocks, and mechanical injuries.

When the pericardium is removed and observed thoroughly, the heart consists of three chambers where two anterior chambers are called auricles or atria and a posterior pink coloured conical chamber is called ventricle. In addition to the auricles and ventricle, frog has two additional chambers known as sinus venosus and truncus arteriosus. Sinus venosus present dorsally and truncus arteriosus present ventrally.

On the dorsal side, heart shows a thin walled, dark coloured and triangular chamber which is called sinus venosus. Sinus venosus is formed by the union of three caval veins in which two are anterior precavals and one is posterior post caval. Sinus venosus receives impure blood from various parts of body through precaval and postcaval veins to pour into right auricle. Two pulmonary veins from lungs also unite and open into the left auricle of the heart.

On the ventral side, there is a tubular structure arising from the anterior margin of ventricle on the right side called truncus arteriosus. It runs anteriorly and divides into two branches called right aortic trunk and left aortic trunk. Each aortic trunk further gives off three branches namely- carotid arch, systemic arch and pulmo-cutaneous arch. Right and Left auricles are separated externally by a faint inter-auricular groove and two auricles are separated from the ventricle by a transverse groove called coronary sulcus.

2. Internal structure The internal structure of heart can be observed and studied by removing its ventral wall. It shows that it is a hollow conical muscular organ with two thin walled auricles and a thickwalled ventricle.

Figure 8.4.16 Internal Structure of heart of frog Right and left auricles are separated from each other by a thin and vertical inter auricular septum. The right auricle is larger and receives blood from sinus venosus through a transverse oval shaped sinu-atrial opening, guarded by valve formed of two flaps like structures. Sinuatrial or sinu-auricular opening is situated medially near interauricular septum. The common opening of pulmonary veins is situated in the left auricle near the septum but it is without valve. Both the auricles open into a single ventricle by a common wide auriculo-ventricular aperture, which is guarded by valve made up of four flaps; one dorsal, one ventral and two lateral in position. The free edges of these flaps project into the ventricle and are supported by fine contractile but tough thread-like structures known as chordate tendineae. The chordae tendineae regulate the movement of the auriculo-ventricular valve to allow the blood to pass Biology, Grade 11 | 406
from the auricles into the ventricle but prevent the backward flow of blood from ventricle into the auricles.

The wall of ventricle is thick hence highly muscular and spongy and its inner surface contains numerous ridges and strands called the columnae carneae. The spaces between these strands are called fissures. Ventricle on the right side opens into truncus arteriosus on the ventral side. A row of three semilunar valves is present at the opening where ventricle opens into truncus arteriosus. These valves allow the flow of blood into the truncus arteriosus from the ventricle.
